title: Gautami, the snake, Death and Time
hookLine: a hunter drags a snake to a grieving mother so she can watch it die, and she tells him to let it go
carry: karma is a long chain, and you're one link
tomorrow: the sun turns north. how will Bhishma choose to go?

lines: A BOY BITTEN BY A SNAKE.
cards: After all of Bhishma's teaching, Yudhishthira is still stuck in the same place. I caused all this, he says. I'm the reason you're lying on those arrows.
So when the Anushasana Parva opens, Bhishma answers with a story about blame. An old woman named Gautami finds her son dead. A snake has bitten him.
A hunter, Arjunaka, catches the snake, ties it with a cord, and drags it to her. Tell me how to kill it, he says. Fire, or cut it to pieces?

teach.b: Gautami says: let it go. Killing it won't bring my son back, and it won't make me any less sad. The hunter argues; surely the guilty should pay.
Then the snake speaks up. Don't blame me. I didn't act on my own.
Death sent me. And Death, Mrityu, appears. Don't blame me either.
I was directed by Time. Then Time itself, Kala, arrives and says: none of us is the real cause. The boy's own past actions, his karma, brought him here.

We were only the instruments. Gautami accepts it, and the hunter lets the snake go. Each link points at the next, and the chain ends not in a villain but in the long working of actions and their results.
That's karma as this story sees it: not a scoreboard kept on one person, but a long chain of many actions, many hands, running back further than anyone can see. Now look at who's listening.
Yudhishthira is sure he's the snake, that the deaths are on him alone.

teach.h: YOU ARE ONE LINK, NOT THE WHOLE OF IT
teach.b: Bhishma is saying, gently, that you are one link in something much longer, and you are not the whole of it. This isn't permission to stop caring. It's a way out of the guilt that eats a person alive and helps nobody.
And notice who sees it first. Not the warrior, not the king. A grieving old mother, with every reason to want revenge.
When grief says it was all my fault, Bhishma's answer is gentler and harder: own your link honestly, and don't claim the whole chain.

how: The story of Gautami, the snake, Death and Time is retold by Hindu teachers when they speak of karma and of letting go of revenge, and it stands at the opening of the Anushasana Parva.

o: a hunter's right to punish a guilty animal
instruction: the book that follows Shanti
the order Time gives to Death and the snake

games.q: the chain of blame — tap the pairs.

s: Gautami asked the hunter to kill the snake
she told him to let it go; killing it wouldn't bring her son back.
Death blamed Time for the boy's death
Death said it was directed by Time, and Time pointed to the boy's karma.
Bhishma tells the story to Yudhishthira about his guilt
Yudhishthira believed the deaths were on him alone.

games.q: a friend says: 'karma means either it's all my fault, or it's all fate and nothing i do matters.' by Gautami's story, what fits?
o: karma is a long chain of many actions: own your link, and don't carry the whole chain.
games.why: the snake, Death and Time each point onward. Bhishma tells the story to free Yudhishthira from a guilt that claims too much, not to stop him caring.

practice: Soften your jaw and bring to mind something you still blame yourself for, and look honestly at your part in it.
Then, breath by breath, let the other causes come into view, other people, timing, things nobody chose; you don't have to excuse anything, just let the picture be its true size.
If you pray, you can bring that weight into your prayer.
